PROCEDURE: the six phases PATTERNS, BUILD, HARDEN, SIBLINGS, SELF-REVIEW and CLASSIFY, in this order.
Each phase after BUILD, while it works, runs only a targeted test of the code it changes, such as one
test file, when the repo has one, and never the gate. A phase with nothing to do for this round's changes is
skipped, such as HARDEN after a change to comments alone, or SIBLINGS when the round made no fix.
When any phase after BUILD changed code, run the gate once more under BUILD's rules after the last such
phase and before CLASSIFY. That run's outcome is the one you report. When no phase after BUILD changed
code, BUILD's run is the one you report.
Use the tools you have, such as web search or a browser, to check how something behaves, and run the project to see a change working when the project says how to run it and the run writes nothing in the repo.
1. PATTERNS: before you write code, find how the repo already does the same kind of thing, such
   as its names, data shapes and error path, and follow it where the block does not prescribe otherwise.
2. BUILD: READ E:/flow/runs/flow/acceptance-review-block-a-r1.md
   and route every finding and gap in it, at every tier, through the DECISION MATRIX below: fix it or
   log it. A review is another agent's claim. For each finding and gap, confirm it yourself against the current code, by reading the place it cites and following the input or path it names, or by running the check it names. A finding you refute is dropped under the DECISION MATRIX's false-positive rule (1), with the file:line that refutes it. Its suggested fix is a hint, never an instruction. Before you apply any part of it, check it against the text it changes, the block's text and every sibling text that must agree with it, such as other call sites, the same string or rule elsewhere, and the docs that describe the behavior. Confirm any command, flag or behavior it relies on that the repo does not already use the same way. Build the fix that closes the confirmed cause, which may differ from the suggestion. A finding raised as "CONTESTS DISMISSAL" follows the DECISION MATRIX's rule for a contested dismissal, never rule 1. A gap for a wrong risk answer, for a sweep line that is missing, leaves out a hit the change left wrong, or disagrees with the change, or for a path that changed after its round's snapshot, follows its own rule below. A gap for a wrong risk answer, for a sweep line that is missing, leaves out a hit the change left wrong, or disagrees with the change, or for a path that changed after its round's snapshot, takes no fix and no log, since the blind review its verdict triggers judges the entire block diff.
   Then RUN THE GATE until it is GREEN — build: npm run build ; verification: per
   the plan's Test Strategy (npm test). Also run the FULL suite to confirm you did not redden it (report full_suite_outcome). When the verification command is already the full suite, its one run counts for both, and full_suite_outcome reports that run. Never
   weaken/delete tests to get green. SANITY-CHECK the runner really executed your unit tests.
   Run each gate command this step names with the shell tool's timeout set to its maximum (600000 ms), and write its entire output to E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/gate-develop-block-a-r2-<build or test>.log, replacing that log's earlier content. Then read the end of that log and the command's exit code. A gate that may outlast that timeout runs through the shell tool's own background option, never with a shell `&`, since a job started with `&` may stop when its tool call returns. It writes the same log, and once the command exits, its exit code to E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/gate-develop-block-a-r2-<build or test>.exit, which you delete before you start it. Wait for it with one bounded loop in the foreground that checks every 10 seconds whether that exit-code file exists and stops when it does or after 9 minutes, so it ends inside the shell tool's timeout. Run that loop again until the file exists, then read the exit code and the end of the log once.
3. HARDEN: in the code this round added or changed, handle edge cases, handle each expected failure
   with a message that names its cause, log where the repo logs, add a test for each risky path, and
   clean up the code you wrote, at every tier of the SEVERITY scale below.
4. SIBLINGS: when you FIX a finding in any phase or make a fix this block requires, grep for
   every sibling path with the same mechanism, and fix each one the ZONE ROUTING above fixes.
   DROP + LOG every other sibling by its file:line, or log the class it belongs to. A sibling in code
   this block's text excludes, or that another block of the plan owns, is DROP + LOG wherever it lies,
   in the SPEC reason form below.
5. SELF-REVIEW: before you return, apply the SEVERITY scale, the REACH step and the CHECKLIST
   below to the code this round changed or read: the part of your unstaged diff, new files included, that
   this round changed, and the code you read in this round, such as the callers and consumers the REACH
   step names. Code that earlier rounds changed and that this round neither changed nor read is out of
   this phase's scope, since each earlier round's self-review judged that round's code, and each blind
   review judges the entire block diff.
   Hunt the task code in that scope for every finding at every tier. In the connected code in that
   scope, check your change's effects. Route each finding through the ZONE ROUTING above and the
   DECISION MATRIX below.
   In the REACH step, skip a sibling grep that the SIBLINGS phase already ran on the same code in this round.
   A regression here is a behavior of the accepted baseline that the acceptance check below counts as
   regressed, or a comment or doc sentence that was true in the accepted baseline and that this cycle's diff made false.
   After the blind review, when one runs, acceptance checks that every acceptance criterion of this block holds with a file:line, test or command-output locator, that the feature is reachable from real entry points, that every earlier review finding is closed or declined, that no behavior of the accepted baseline regressed, that each risk answer of a round no blind review judged holds against that round's own hunks, that the sweep of the latest such round lists each changed name or phrase of that round's hunks and each hit it marks unaffected still agrees with the change and a rerun of each line's search finds no hit the line leaves out that the change left wrong, that the tree it stages differs from the snapshot your CLASSIFY phase returns only in untracked build output or a cache that a gate or test run regenerates, and that the gate is satisfied. Acceptance does not count as regressed a removed defect (a real defect that an earlier review finding names, or the same defect on a sibling path of such a finding or of a fix this block requires) that lies in code this block's text does not exclude and in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code. Nor does it count a removed defect that a FOCUSED line in DECISIONS.md names and that lies in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code.
SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.
6. CLASSIFY: judge the risk of each change this round made, in any phase, under the RISK
   QUESTIONS below. Write E:/flow/runs/flow/risk-block-a-r2.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/ if needed). The file may hold an earlier launch's text, so Read it first, if it exists, and then replace its entire content. Its first line is
   `Snapshot: <tree id>`, the tree id of a snapshot of the working tree. Take the snapshot after your
   last change, with these commands, which write a temporary index file (create E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/ if
   needed) and never the real index. The last command prints the tree id, which you also return as risk_snapshot:
     cp "$(git -C E:/repo rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path index)" "E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r2.index"
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r2.index" git -C E:/repo add -A
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r2.index" git -C E:/repo write-tree
   Delete the temporary index file once the last command has printed the tree id. After the first line, write one section per change, named by its file:line, with its four answers.
   Then write a `## Sweep` section. For each function, constant, field, message or rule phrase this round changed,
   list the search you ran and each hit, marked `updated` or `unaffected` with a few words of reason. A
   changed field, return value, file format or output that other code or prompts read lists those readers as hits. A
   change that adds, removes or renames a field of an agent's return schema also lists as hits each sentence in the repo's prose that lists that agent's return fields, such as "returns", "only" and "nothing else". A
   round that changed nothing writes "No changes." and no `## Sweep` section. Return review_needed=true when any change is not low
   risk, and false only when every change is low risk. With false, the engine may send this round's diff to
   acceptance with no blind review, and acceptance then checks each answer against that round's hunks.
RISK QUESTIONS - answer each one for a change:
  - Systems: does the change need edits in more than one system to stay consistent?
  - Paths: does it add or change many branches, loops, error paths or state transitions?
  - Critical code: does it touch data writes, deletion, security, concurrency, a public contract, or code
    whose behavior is hard to follow?
  - Assumptions: does it rest on a judgment call or an assumption that an input, a platform or a caller
    could falsify?
Each answer cites its evidence, such as a file:line or a count of the branches or systems the change adds
or touches, or is "no". A doubtful answer counts as yes. A change is low risk when every answer is no.
7. LEAVE EVERYTHING UNSTAGED — do NOT `git add` content and do NOT commit. EXCEPTION: for any file
   you CREATE, run `git -C E:/repo add -N <file>` (intent-to-add, so reviewers' `git diff` sees it;
   it does not stage content). Set unstaged_confirmed=true. Anything YOU stage is reviewed by nobody
   and HALTS the run. The staged index already holds the blocks this run accepted before this one.
   Leave the index as it is: never unstage, restage or revert those blocks. You may still edit any file
   this block needs, including one an earlier block changed.
8. DECISION MATRIX — for each ambiguity or finding, route it yourself IN ORDER (first match wins):
  1. Not a real problem / false positive → DROP + LOG.
  2. A pre-existing finding, at any tier, that the ZONE ROUTING above does not fix → DROP + LOG.
      Never fix it (regression risk).
  3. Stops the build/tests/verification → FIX it where the ZONE ROUTING above places the fix, or
      ESCALATE it (7) where that routing says to.
  4. A finding the ZONE ROUTING above fixes, at any tier, that does not conflict with the plan → FIX.
      A conflict with the plan still goes to 6a or 6b.
  5. Needed to satisfy the spec / wire this block in → FIX (an unreachable or incomplete block is not done).
      A piece the plan's prescribed text leaves out is this case, not a conflict, so it takes no amendment.
      An exception to a rule the plan states is a conflict (6a or 6b), never a left-out piece.
  6a. Conflicts with the plan AND you VERIFIED that what the plan PRESCRIBES is itself defective (you
      reproduced it, or demonstrated the failure path, to the same evidence bar as any FIX)
      → FIX it: the verified defect outranks the prescription. LOG an amendment.
      PRECEDENCE — that verified defect also outranks the "NO scope creep beyond the plan and the fixes the ZONE ROUTING below allows"
      instruction above and the CONVENTIONS rubric. Everywhere else the plan and the conventions
      still bind.
  6b. Conflicts with the plan, and you did not verify that the plan's prescription is defective
      → DROP + LOG, in the SPEC reason form below. The DROP reason names the read or probe that showed
      the prescription works as written. A conflict that no read or probe settles goes to 7.
  7. A choice that changes user-visible behavior, stored data or a public contract, and that the plan,
      the code, the CONVENTIONS and a quick check cannot settle, OR a blocker you cannot resolve in scope
      → ESCALATE + LOG. Settle any other open choice yourself under 4, 5 or 8.
  8. Any other open choice: weigh its benefit (what it improves, and how likely an input reaches it)
      against its cost (diff size, regression risk, scope). Benefit clearly ahead → FIX. Benefit not
      clearly ahead, or a different block's work → DROP + LOG.
  • Every finding a review names ends FIXED, LOGGED to the DISMISSED file, AMENDED (6a) or ESCALATED (7). None is dropped silently.
  • A finding a reviewer RE-RAISED as "CONTESTS DISMISSAL": do NOT re-drop it — FIX it, or if it is
    truly a user-only call, ESCALATE it. A contested pre-existing finding that the ZONE ROUTING above
    does not fix goes to 7, with the default of leaving it unchanged, since that routing bounds every
    change you make. NEVER log the same dismissal twice.
  • A REGRESSION that a review of this block names, a blind review included, or that the acceptance review
    counted, and that you confirm against the code, or one your SELF-REVIEW found, is a bug, so never DROP
    it under 1, 2, 6b or 8. FIX it at any tier (6a when the fix conflicts with the plan), or ESCALATE it (7)
    with the default you took when only a change in other code closes it. A named regression you refute is
    dropped under rule 1 with the file:line that refutes it, as for any refuted review finding.
    A regression that a construction the block's text prescribes causes is fixed under 6a, with an
    amendment that cites the regression as its defect evidence. When that fix would change a choice that
    the block's text says the user made, it goes to rule 7's branch that cannot proceed, so the
    block parks with the user's question in E:/flow/runs/flow/question-block-a.md.

LOGGING is your ONLY output besides code. Keep it minimal and unambiguous:
  • DROP (1, 2, 6b or 8): append ONE terse line to E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/DISMISSED-block-a.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/ if it does not exist):
      `<file:line, or the class of places it covers> — <finding gist> — SKIPPED: <reason, ≤15 words>`
    Name one place by its file:line, or the class of places the line covers, such as every caller of a
    function. The reason must hold for every place the line names.
    The blind reviewer cannot read the plan, so the reason must be decidable from the code alone: never
    cite a plan id, block id, issue id or plan clause. One reason form is the exception, for a decline
    whose reason is that the plan prescribes the code, this block's text excludes it, or another block of the plan owns it. Its entire line is:
      `<file:line> — <finding gist> — SKIPPED: SPEC: <file:line of that code> — <which of the three holds, and the read or probe that showed it, ≤15 words>`
    Its reason names the code's file:line and quotes no plan text. The blind reviewer skips such a line, and
    acceptance checks it against the plan.
    A false-positive reason cites the file:line that refutes the finding.
    Every SKIPPED reason states a fact you checked this round: the file and line you read, or the command you
    ran and its output. A finding you can neither confirm nor refute is never dropped. Settle it with a
    read or a probe, fix it, or escalate it (7).
  • RECORD (2 or SIBLINGS): when you DROP + LOG a real pre-existing defect at low or above
    in code no other block of the plan owns, under rule 2 or as a sibling path the SIBLINGS phase leaves unchanged, also
    append ONE entry for it
    to E:/flow/backlog/repo-0a1b2c3d/flow-block-a-d48cf78a.md only.
    Count it in backlog_entries and name "block-a" in backlog_blocks.
    Write the defect's DISMISSED line too, since the blind reviewer reads that file and never this one.
    A false positive and a nit dropped under rule 2 or SIBLINGS get no entry.
    A new file starts with the four lines "## Plan: flow-block-a-d48cf78a - backlog from block block-a of run flow", "mode: fix", "gate: green" and "status: todo", then a blank line. An existing file keeps its header, and a new entry goes below its last entry. When the file's "status:" line reads skip, set it to todo, since the backlog build takes only todo and done files.
    Before you append, create E:/flow/backlog/repo-0a1b2c3d/ if it does not exist, then grep the *.md files in E:/flow/backlog/repo-0a1b2c3d/ for the path of the file the new entry names and for the name of the function or identifier at the defect, and read each entry that a grep matches. Never append a defect that an entry there with "- status: open" or "- status: needs-attention" already holds. When the only entries that hold it say "- status: fixed" or "- status: stale", the defect is back in the code, so append a new entry whose **What:** names their ids.
    Each entry copies the shape of debug's issue files, with n one past the highest n in that file's entry ids:
      ### [flow-block-a-d48cf78a-<n>] <title>
      - id: flow-block-a-d48cf78a-<n>
      - status: open
      - file: <path>:<line>
      - severity: <low | medium | high | critical>
      - category: <category>
      - size: <trivial | small | medium | large>
      - decision: <ACTIONABLE | NEEDS_USER>
      **What:** <the defect, the input or path that reaches it, and its harm>
      **Fix:** <the change that closes it>
    A DISMISSED line that covers a class of places gets one entry. Its "- file:" line names the first
    place, and its **What:** names the class.
    Set the entry's "- decision:" line by one rule. ACTIONABLE when the entry is a defect or a cleanup with one clear fix, its size is trivial or small, and the fix changes no user-visible behavior, stored data or public contract. NEEDS_USER otherwise, such as a feature, a refactor, a choice between fixes, or a fix that changes user-visible behavior. A later run builds an ACTIONABLE entry without triage, and a NEEDS_USER entry waits for the user.
    When you append a FOCUSED line below, grep the *.md files in E:/flow/backlog/repo-0a1b2c3d/ for the path of the file the fix changes and for the name of the function or identifier at the fix, and read each entry that a grep matches.
    When an entry that a grep matches holds the defect that line's fix closes, add one line after that entry's
    **Fix:** line in that file:
      **Closed by:** block block-a r2 of run flow. Confirm before the entry is built that the accepted baseline holds the fix.
    Leave its status and decision as they are, since a park clears the fix from the tree.
  • RETIRED (a backlog entry the block retires): when the block's text names a backlog entry as retired or superseded,
    grep the *.md files in E:/flow/backlog/repo-0a1b2c3d/ for that entry's id and add one line after its **Fix:** line, with the
    block's change as the fix:
      **Closed by:** block block-a r2 of run flow. Confirm before the entry is built that the accepted baseline holds the fix.
    Leave its status and decision as they are, since a park clears the change from the tree.
  • FEATURE (both change policies): append ONE entry for each feature or refactor you noticed that lies outside
    this block's scope, in code no other block of the plan owns, instead of building it. Route, count, dedup and number it as a RECORD entry. It
    takes RECORD's shape with "- category: feature", "- decision: NEEDS_USER" and no "- severity:" line.
    Its **What:** names the feature or refactor, the code it touches and what it adds or improves.
  • AMEND (6a): append ONE entry to E:/flow/runs/flow/AMENDED-block-a.md:
      `## Plan amendment: block-a r2, launch 1`
      then the plan clause you overrode (QUOTED verbatim), the defect (file:line + one line on why it is
      real), and what you built instead.
    Then append ONE POINTER line to E:/flow/runs/flow/DECISIONS.md: the block id, the round, the launch, the defect's
    file:line, and the path E:/flow/runs/flow/AMENDED-block-a.md, with NO plan text. Count every entry you wrote in plan_amendments.
  • ESCALATE (7), in one of two branches:
    - You CANNOT proceed without the answer: append a FULL, self-contained entry to E:/flow/runs/flow/question-block-a.md (all
      the detail the user needs to decide) under the heading `## Question: block-a r2`, and set
      needs_user=true (this block stops and is parked, and the park copies the entry into its backlog entry).
    - You can proceed with a defensible default: append an entry to E:/flow/runs/flow/DECISIONS.md (the choice, the
      options, the default you took and why), leave needs_user=false, AND append ONE terse line to
      E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/DISMISSED-block-a.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/ if it does not exist) in the DROP shape above, its reason
      `ESCALATED: <the default you took, ≤15 words>`, because the blind reviewer is NOT shown E:/flow/runs/flow/DECISIONS.md
      and would re-raise your default every round until this block parks.
      Also append ONE backlog entry for it when the choice lies in code no other block of the plan owns, routed, counted, deduped and
      numbered as a RECORD entry. It takes RECORD's shape with "- category: decision", "- decision: NEEDS_USER"
      and no "- severity:" line. Its **What:** states the question and the default you took, and its **Fix:**
      states the other option. When the default lies in code this block's diff adds or changes, add the line
      "**Parked with:** block block-a. Hold this entry until that block is done or skip." after the **Fix:** line, since a park removes that code from the tree.
    Write to E:/flow/runs/flow/question-block-a.md only a question the user must answer before a block can finish. Never write an
    informational note, a test observation, a chore or a default you took to it.
  • FOCUSED (this run's change policy): append ONE line to E:/flow/runs/flow/DECISIONS.md for each fix of a defect already in the accepted baseline
    that you made, in any zone, without a criterion of this block requiring it, and that no earlier round
    logged, naming its file:line, what changed and why:
      `FOCUSED block-a: <file:line> — <what changed> — <why>`
This is NOT a general code review. Make THIS block correct, testable and production-safe, make the
fixes the ZONE ROUTING allows, and touch nothing else.
Return ONLY the decision fields via the schema (no prose report).

   the runner really executed your unit tests. Some runners silently ignore extra path args, so when in

Then read the end of that log and the command's exit code. A gate that may outlast that timeout runs through the shell tool's own background option, never with a shell `&`, since a job started with `&` may stop when its tool call returns. It writes the same log, and once the command exits, its exit code to E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/gate-develop-block-b-r2-<build or test>.exit, which you delete before you start it. Wait for it with one bounded loop in the foreground that checks every 10 seconds whether that exit-code file exists and stops when it does or after 9 minutes, so it ends inside the shell tool's timeout. Run that loop again until the file exists, then read the exit code and the end of the log once.

5. SELF-REVIEW: before you return, apply the SEVERITY scale, the REACH step and the CHECKLIST
   below to the code this round changed or read: the part of your unstaged diff, new files included, that
   this round changed, and the code you read in this round, such as the callers and consumers the REACH
   step names. Code that earlier rounds changed and that this round neither changed nor read is out of
   this phase's scope, since each earlier round's self-review judged that round's code, and each blind
   review judges the entire block diff.
   Hunt the task code in that scope for every finding at every tier. In the connected code in that
   scope, check your change's effects. Route each finding through the ZONE ROUTING above and the
   DECISION MATRIX below.
   In the REACH step, skip a sibling grep that the SIBLINGS phase already ran on the same code in this round.
   A regression here is a behavior of the accepted baseline that the acceptance check below counts as
   regressed, or a comment or doc sentence that was true in the accepted baseline and that this cycle's diff made false.
   After the blind review, when one runs, acceptance checks that every acceptance criterion of this block holds with a file:line, test or command-output locator, that every call site this block owns is converted, that every earlier review finding is closed or declined, that no behavior of the accepted baseline regressed, that each risk answer of a round no blind review judged holds against that round's own hunks, that the sweep of the latest such round lists each changed name or phrase of that round's hunks and each hit it marks unaffected still agrees with the change and a rerun of each line's search finds no hit the line leaves out that the change left wrong, that the tree it stages differs from the snapshot your CLASSIFY phase returns only in untracked build output or a cache that a gate or test run regenerates, and that this block's gate meets its expectation. Acceptance does not count as regressed a removed defect (a real defect that an earlier review finding names, or the same defect on a sibling path of such a finding or of a fix this block requires) that lies in code this block's text does not exclude and in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code. Nor does it count a removed defect that a FOCUSED line in DECISIONS.md names and that lies in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code.
SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.
6. CLASSIFY: judge the risk of each change this round made, in any phase, under the RISK
   QUESTIONS below. Write E:/flow/runs/flow/risk-block-b-r2.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/ if needed). The file may hold an earlier launch's text, so Read it first, if it exists, and then replace its entire content. Its first line is
   `Snapshot: <tree id>`, the tree id of a snapshot of the working tree. Take the snapshot after your
   last change, with these commands, which write a temporary index file (create E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/ if
   needed) and never the real index. The last command prints the tree id, which you also return as risk_snapshot:
     cp "$(git -C E:/repo rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path index)" "E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r2.index"
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r2.index" git -C E:/repo add -A
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r2.index" git -C E:/repo write-tree
   Delete the temporary index file once the last command has printed the tree id. After the first line, write one section per change, named by its file:line, with its four answers.
   Then write a `## Sweep` section. For each function, constant, field, message or rule phrase this round changed,
   list the search you ran and each hit, marked `updated` or `unaffected` with a few words of reason. A
   changed field, return value, file format or output that other code or prompts read lists those readers as hits. A
   change that adds, removes or renames a field of an agent's return schema also lists as hits each sentence in the repo's prose that lists that agent's return fields, such as "returns", "only" and "nothing else". A
   round that changed nothing writes "No changes." and no `## Sweep` section. Return review_needed=true when any change is not low
   risk, and false only when every change is low risk. With false, the engine may send this round's diff to
   acceptance with no blind review, and acceptance then checks each answer against that round's hunks.
RISK QUESTIONS - answer each one for a change:
  - Systems: does the change need edits in more than one system to stay consistent?
  - Paths: does it add or change many branches, loops, error paths or state transitions?
  - Critical code: does it touch data writes, deletion, security, concurrency, a public contract, or code
    whose behavior is hard to follow?
  - Assumptions: does it rest on a judgment call or an assumption that an input, a platform or a caller
    could falsify?
Each answer cites its evidence, such as a file:line or a count of the branches or systems the change adds
or touches, or is "no". A doubtful answer counts as yes. A change is low risk when every answer is no.
7. LEAVE EVERYTHING UNSTAGED — do NOT `git add` content and do NOT commit. EXCEPTION: for any file
   you CREATE, run `git -C E:/repo add -N <file>` (intent-to-add, so reviewers' `git diff` sees it;
   it does not stage content). Set unstaged_confirmed=true. Anything YOU stage is reviewed by nobody
   and HALTS the run. The staged index already holds the blocks this run accepted before this one.
   Leave the index as it is: never unstage, restage or revert those blocks. You may still edit any file
   this block needs, including one an earlier block changed.
8. DECISION MATRIX — for each ambiguity or finding, route it yourself IN ORDER (first match wins):
  1. Not a real problem / false positive → DROP + LOG.
  2. A pre-existing finding, at any tier, that the ZONE ROUTING above does not fix → DROP + LOG.
      Never fix it (regression risk).
  3. Stops the build/tests/verification → FIX it where the ZONE ROUTING above places the fix, or
      ESCALATE it (7) where that routing says to.
  4. A finding the ZONE ROUTING above fixes, at any tier, that does not conflict with the plan → FIX.
      A conflict with the plan still goes to 6a or 6b.
  5. Needed to satisfy the spec / wire this block in → FIX (an unreachable or incomplete block is not done).
      A piece the plan's prescribed text leaves out is this case, not a conflict, so it takes no amendment.
      An exception to a rule the plan states is a conflict (6a or 6b), never a left-out piece.
  6a. Conflicts with the plan AND you VERIFIED that what the plan PRESCRIBES is itself defective (you
      reproduced it, or demonstrated the failure path, to the same evidence bar as any FIX)
      → FIX it: the verified defect outranks the prescription. LOG an amendment.
      PRECEDENCE — that verified defect also outranks the "NO scope creep beyond this block and the fixes the ZONE ROUTING below allows"
      instruction above and the CONVENTIONS rubric. Everywhere else the plan and the conventions
      still bind.
  6b. Conflicts with the plan, and you did not verify that the plan's prescription is defective
      → DROP + LOG, in the SPEC reason form below. The DROP reason names the read or probe that showed
      the prescription works as written. A conflict that no read or probe settles goes to 7.
  7. A choice that changes user-visible behavior, stored data or a public contract, and that the plan,
      the code, the CONVENTIONS and a quick check cannot settle, OR a blocker you cannot resolve in scope
      → ESCALATE + LOG. Settle any other open choice yourself under 4, 5 or 8.
  8. Any other open choice: weigh its benefit (what it improves, and how likely an input reaches it)
      against its cost (diff size, regression risk, scope). Benefit clearly ahead → FIX. Benefit not
      clearly ahead, or a different block's work → DROP + LOG.
  • Every finding a review names ends FIXED, LOGGED to the DISMISSED file, AMENDED (6a) or ESCALATED (7). None is dropped silently.
  • A finding a reviewer RE-RAISED as "CONTESTS DISMISSAL": do NOT re-drop it — FIX it, or if it is
    truly a user-only call, ESCALATE it. A contested pre-existing finding that the ZONE ROUTING above

    change you make. NEVER log the same dismissal twice.
  • A REGRESSION that a review of this block names, a blind review included, or that the acceptance review

    with the default you took when only a change in other code closes it. A named regression you refute is

LOGGING is your ONLY output besides code. Keep it minimal and unambiguous:

CODE ZONES - every piece of code lies in one of three zones:

  - Other code: everything else.

  - Task code: hunt it, and fix every finding in it at every tier, a defect the accepted baseline already

  - Connected code: fix a finding the diff introduces or exposes there.

PROCEDURE: the six phases PATTERNS, BUILD, HARDEN, SIBLINGS, SELF-REVIEW and CLASSIFY, in this order.
Each phase after BUILD, while it works, runs only a targeted test of the code it changes, such as one
test file, when the repo has one, and never the gate. A phase with nothing to do for this round's changes is
skipped, such as HARDEN after a change to comments alone, or SIBLINGS when the round made no fix.
When any phase after BUILD changed code, run the gate once more under BUILD's rules after the last such
phase and before CLASSIFY. That run's outcome is the one you report. When no phase after BUILD changed
code, BUILD's run is the one you report.
Use the tools you have, such as web search or a browser, to check how something behaves, and run the project to see a change working when the project says how to run it and the run writes nothing in the repo.
1. PATTERNS: before you write code, find how the repo already does the same kind of thing, such

Then read the end of that log and the command's exit code. A gate that may outlast that timeout runs through the shell tool's own background option, never with a shell `&`, since a job started with `&` may stop when its tool call returns. It writes the same log, and once the command exits, its exit code to E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/gate-develop-block-a-r6-<build or test>.exit, which you delete before you start it. Wait for it with one bounded loop in the foreground that checks every 10 seconds whether that exit-code file exists and stops when it does or after 9 minutes, so it ends inside the shell tool's timeout. 5. SELF-REVIEW: before you return, apply the SEVERITY scale, the REACH step and the CHECKLIST

   this round changed, and the code you read in this round, such as the callers and consumers the REACH
   step names. Code that earlier rounds changed and that this round neither changed nor read is out of

   Hunt the task code in that scope for every finding at every tier. In the connected code in that
   scope, check your change's effects. Route each finding through the ZONE ROUTING above and the

   In the REACH step, skip a sibling grep that the SIBLINGS phase already ran on the same code in this round.
   A regression here is a behavior of the accepted baseline that the acceptance check below counts as
   regressed, or a comment or doc sentence that was true in the accepted baseline and that this cycle's diff made false.
   After the blind review, when one runs, acceptance checks that every acceptance criterion of this block holds with a file:line, test or command-output locator, that the feature is reachable from real entry points, that every earlier review finding is closed or declined, that no behavior of the accepted baseline regressed, that each risk answer of a round no blind review judged holds against that round's own hunks, that the sweep of the latest such round lists each changed name or phrase of that round's hunks and each hit it marks unaffected still agrees with the change and a rerun of each line's search finds no hit the line leaves out that the change left wrong, that the tree it stages differs from the snapshot your CLASSIFY phase returns only in untracked build output or a cache that a gate or test run regenerates, and that the gate is satisfied. Acceptance does not count as regressed a removed defect (a real defect that an earlier review finding names, or the same defect on a sibling path of such a finding or of a fix this block requires) that lies in code this block's text does not exclude and in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code. Nor does it count a removed defect that a FOCUSED line in DECISIONS.md names and that lies in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code.
SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.
6. CLASSIFY: judge the risk of each change this round made, in any phase, under the RISK
   QUESTIONS below. Write E:/flow/runs/flow/risk-block-a-r6.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/ if needed). The file may hold an earlier launch's text, so Read it first, if it exists, and then replace its entire content. Its first line is
   `Snapshot: <tree id>`, the tree id of a snapshot of the working tree. Take the snapshot after your
   last change, with these commands, which write a temporary index file (create E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/ if
   needed) and never the real index. The last command prints the tree id, which you also return as risk_snapshot:
     cp "$(git -C E:/repo rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path index)" "E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r6.index"

You are a CODE CRITIC. You have NO information about what this code is for or should do, and no plan,
spec or goal. Do not seek any. Judge the code PURELY ON ITS OWN MERITS.

This is the closing pass, numbered round 6 in its file names, after round 5 of at most 5. Round numbers count develop rounds, so a later stage has no file for a round that an earlier stage sent back. Of the rounds that reach the blind review stage, the blind review runs on the block's first one in this launch, and on a later one only when a round since the block's last blind review judged a change not low risk or gave no judgment, or an acceptance verdict since then found a risk judgment wrong. Every other round has no blind review file. The closing pass, the one developer pass that follows round 5 when that round ends without acceptance staging the block, reaches the blind review stage whatever its gate, and no develop round follows it. A round file of this block that this prompt does not name may come from an earlier launch of the block, so ignore it.
TARGET REPO: E:/repo
GATES — already ran before you were spawned, and a later stage re-runs them before anything is staged.
Never run them in full. Run the test command only for ONE targeted test that confirms a suspected defect.
  build: npm run build
  test:  npm test
Any other command that writes nothing in the repo, such as a tool's check mode, and a probe script in a
temporary folder outside the repo and outside the folder that holds E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/ are allowed.
Use the tools you have, such as web search or a browser, to check how something behaves, and run the project to see a change working when the project says how to run it and the run writes nothing in the repo.
CONVENTIONS (judge against these): (none supplied — infer from the surrounding code)

Settled decisions: E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/DISMISSED-block-a.md does not exist, so nothing is settled yet. Do not search for it elsewhere.
Do NOT read prior review files, apart from the overwrite read the WRITE step names. Review the CURRENT
diff FRESH, catching new or nearby issues.

SCOPE — review ONLY this cycle's UNSTAGED work:
  Read the diff in this order, and never run the entire `git diff` at once:
  1. `git -C E:/repo diff --stat`.
  2. `git -C E:/repo diff -- <file>` for each file it lists, one file per command.
  3. `git -C E:/repo status --porcelain`, then READ every untracked file (`??`), since `git diff` OMITS those.
  A ` A` entry (intent-to-add) is a new file `git diff` already shows in full. A first-column `A` or
  `M` is STAGED: the staged half of an `AM` or `MM` file is baseline, and only its unstaged half
  (`git -C E:/repo diff -- <file>`) is this cycle's work.
  `git -C E:/repo diff --staged` is the ACCEPTED baseline — context only, do NOT review it.

SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

Report every finding this diff introduces or exposes, at every tier. Drop silently anything
pre-existing in code the diff neither changes nor interacts with, speculation, and redesigns.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.

HUNT. Working from critical down to nit, find every finding through the CHECKLIST and the REACH
step. A finding at medium or above names the concrete input or path that reaches it and its harm,
cited by file:line. A real defect you cannot tie to a concrete input or path grades low at most. An
EMPTY review is the normal, GOOD outcome.

A hunk that changes ONLY comments, string text or documentation has four checkable defects: a change
to executable code (`git -C E:/repo diff --word-diff` shows each hunk's exact tokens), a path, command,
identifier or file the new text names that does not exist, a sentence the change removed that other
text still refers to, and a claim the new text makes about this repo's code that the code contradicts,
cited by line. Those four checks and the nit list bound your review of such a hunk.
A prompt template or other text an agent or a program acts on is behavior, not string text. Review it
with the full checklist, and grade a contradiction in it by what an agent that follows it would do.

WRITE your findings to E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/quality-review-block-a-r6.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/gate/ if needed). the tree exactly as it is, skip steps 2 and 3, and return saved=false, cleared=false, commit_sha "" and
entry_written=false. A tree that holds no work of this block is not a stop: step 1 says what to do.

1. SAVE. Each command names the repo with `-C`, so it runs from any folder.

      plus this block's unstaged tracked edits and untracked files.

A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or

condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing

Acceptance does not count as regressed a removed defect (a real defect that an earlier review finding names, or the same defect on a sibling path of such a finding or of a fix this block requires) that lies in code this block's text does not exclude and in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code. Nor does it count a removed defect that a FOCUSED line in DECISIONS.md names and that lies in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code.
SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.
6. CLASSIFY: judge the risk of each change this round made, in any phase, under the RISK
   QUESTIONS below. Write E:/flow/runs/flow/risk-block-b-r6.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/ if needed). The file may hold an earlier launch's text, so Read it first, if it exists, and then replace its entire content. Its first line is
   `Snapshot: <tree id>`, the tree id of a snapshot of the working tree. Take the snapshot after your
   last change, with these commands, which write a temporary index file (create E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/ if
   needed) and never the real index. The last command prints the tree id, which you also return as risk_snapshot:
     cp "$(git -C E:/repo rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path index)" "E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r6.index"
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r6.index" git -C E:/repo add -A
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-b-r6.index" git -C E:/repo write-tree
   Delete the temporary index file once the last command has printed the tree id. After the first line, write one section per change, named by its file:line, with its four answers.
   Then write a `## Sweep` section. For each function, constant, field, message or rule phrase this round changed,
   list the search you ran and each hit, marked `updated` or `unaffected` with a few words of reason. A
   changed field, return value, file format or output that other code or prompts read lists those readers as hits. A
   change that adds, removes or renames a field of an agent's return schema also lists as hits each sentence in the repo's prose that lists that agent's return fields, such as "returns", "only" and "nothing else". A
   round that changed nothing writes "No changes." and no `## Sweep` section. Return review_needed=true when any change is not low
   risk, and false only when every change is low risk. With false, the engine may send this round's diff to
   acceptance with no blind review, and acceptance then checks each answer against that round's hunks.
RISK QUESTIONS - answer each one for a change:
  - Systems: does the change need edits in more than one system to stay consistent?
  - Paths: does it add or change many branches, loops, error paths or state transitions?
  - Critical code: does it touch data writes, deletion, security, concurrency, a public contract, or code
    whose behavior is hard to follow?
  - Assumptions: does it rest on a judgment call or an assumption that an input, a platform or a caller
    could falsify?
Each answer cites its evidence, such as a file:line or a count of the branches or systems the change adds
or touches, or is "no". A doubtful answer counts as yes. A change is low risk when every answer is no.
7. LEAVE EVERYTHING UNSTAGED — do NOT `git add` content and do NOT commit. EXCEPTION: for any file

8. DECISION MATRIX — for each ambiguity or finding, route it yourself IN ORDER (first match wins):
  1. Not a real problem / false positive → DROP + LOG.
  2. A pre-existing finding, at any tier, that the ZONE ROUTING above does not fix → DROP + LOG.

  3. Stops the build/tests/verification → FIX it where the ZONE ROUTING above places the fix, or

  4. A finding the ZONE ROUTING above fixes, at any tier, that does not conflict with the plan → FIX.

  8. Any other open choice: weigh its benefit (what it improves, and how likely an input reaches it)
      against its cost (diff size, regression risk, scope). Benefit clearly ahead → FIX. Benefit not
      clearly ahead, or a different block's work → DROP + LOG.

Acceptance does not count as regressed a removed defect (a real defect that an earlier review finding names, or the same defect on a sibling path of such a finding or of a fix this block requires) that lies in code this block's text does not exclude and in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code. Nor does it count a removed defect that a FOCUSED line in DECISIONS.md names and that lies in code no other block of the plan owns, and in task code, in connected code where the change closes a defect the diff introduces or exposes, or in connected code that lies in a function or method that holds task code.
SEVERITY - grade by impact, never by the size of the fix. When two grades fit, take the higher.
  critical - loses or corrupts data, opens a security hole, or breaks the main path on every input.
  high     - crashes or gives wrong output on an input the code accepts.
  medium   - a real defect with a bounded impact, such as a leak, a wrong error path, or a misleading
             result the caller can detect.
  low      - a real defect with no effect on any input the code accepts today.
  nit      - not wrong and no effect on behavior, but it hurts clarity or maintainability.
A comment, docstring, string or doc that is wrong, or that misleads a reader, is a defect graded low or
higher by what the misled reader would do. It is never a nit.
Duplicated logic whose copies already disagree is a defect graded by the harm of the disagreement. It is
never a nit.
A risky path the diff adds with no test, such as an error path, a branch on outside input or a write to
stored state, is a defect graded low or higher. It is never a nit.
NITS include: an overlong comment, or one that restates the code; a comment that breaks the
CONVENTIONS' comment rules; an unclear name, or one inconsistent with its neighbours; dead code the
diff adds (an unused import, variable, parameter, function or branch); a magic number or string with
no named constant; small duplication inside the diff whose copies agree; a redundant line or
condition; control flow nested deeper than its logic needs; a function that mixes I/O with processing
against the CONVENTIONS.

REACH: for every function, constant, field, string or rule the diff changes, grep its callers
and consumers, its sibling paths with the same mechanism, duplicates of the same logic, and every
comment or doc that describes the old behavior. A defect there that the diff introduces or exposes
counts as introduced by this diff. When a fact must be stated in more than one place, keep it in as few
places as possible, at most one copy for users and one for agents, and update every copy in the same change.
A review reports a copy beyond those, or a copy the diff leaves out of date, as a finding.

CHECKLIST:
  - build and tests: anything that breaks the build or tests;
  - correctness and edge cases: empty, missing, blank, multi-valued, unicode, case-folded, huge and
    numeric inputs, platform path forms, and a value computed right but reported wrong;
  - crash-safety and resume: a crash between a state change and its record, a resume that repeats or
    skips a step, a partial write, a leaked temp file or handle, two processes on shared state;
  - error contract: an expected failure that escapes the project's error path, a failure returned in
    a success shape, a message that hides the cause or the way to recover;
  - consistency: the same concept shaped differently from its established counterpart in the repo
    (cite the counterpart's file:line), a problem the repo already solves re-solved another way;
  - completeness: behavior the diff gives some inputs or sibling paths and skips for others, such as
    a container, an enum value, a domain or a cleanup step;
  - tests the diff adds or changes: a test that still passes with the code under test broken, a stub
    that replaces the behavior under test, a risky path the diff adds with no test;
  - prose accuracy: a comment, docstring, string or doc the diff adds or leaves that the code
    contradicts or that now misleads;
  - security, where the diff touches a trust boundary: untrusted input reaching a path, command,
    query or page, a secret reaching a log, result or error;
  - maintainability: the nit list in the scale above.
6. CLASSIFY: judge the risk of each change this round made, in any phase, under the RISK
   QUESTIONS below. Write E:/flow/runs/flow/risk-block-a-r6.md (create E:/flow/runs/flow/ if needed). The file may hold an earlier launch's text, so Read it first, if it exists, and then replace its entire content. Its first line is
   `Snapshot: <tree id>`, the tree id of a snapshot of the working tree. Take the snapshot after your
   last change, with these commands, which write a temporary index file (create E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/ if
   needed) and never the real index. The last command prints the tree id, which you also return as risk_snapshot:
     cp "$(git -C E:/repo rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path index)" "E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r6.index"
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r6.index" git -C E:/repo add -A
     GIT_INDEX_FILE="E:/flow/runs/flow/scratch/snapshot-block-a-r6.index" git -C E:/repo write-tree
   Delete the temporary index file once the last command has printed the tree id. After the first line, write one section per change, named by its file:line, with its four answers.
   Then write a `## Sweep` section. For each function, constant, field, message or rule phrase this round changed,
   list the search you ran and each hit, marked `updated` or `unaffected` with a few words of reason. A
   changed field, return value, file format or output that other code or prompts read lists those readers as hits. A
   change that adds, removes or renames a field of an agent's return schema also lists as hits each sentence in the repo's prose that lists that agent's return fields, such as "returns", "only" and "nothing else". A
   round that changed nothing writes "No changes." and no `## Sweep` section. Return review_needed=true when any change is not low
   risk, and false only when every change is low risk. With false, the engine may send this round's diff to
   acceptance with no blind review, and acceptance then checks each answer against that round's hunks.
RISK QUESTIONS - answer each one for a change:
  - Systems: does the change need edits in more than one system to stay consistent?
  - Paths: does it add or change many branches, loops, error paths or state transitions?
  - Critical code: does it touch data writes, deletion, security, concurrency, a public contract, or code
    whose behavior is hard to follow?
  - Assumptions: does it rest on a judgment call or an assumption that an input, a platform or a caller
    could falsify?
Each answer cites its evidence, such as a file:line or a count of the branches or systems the change adds
or touches, or is "no". A doubtful answer counts as yes. A change is low risk when every answer is no.
7. LEAVE EVERYTHING UNSTAGED — do NOT `git add` content and do NOT commit. EXCEPTION: for any file
   you CREATE, run `git -C E:/repo add -N <file>` (intent-to-add, so reviewers' `git diff` sees it;
   it does not stage content). Set unstaged_confirmed=true. Anything YOU stage is reviewed by nobody
   and HALTS the run. The staged index already holds the blocks this run accepted before this one.
   Leave the index as it is: never unstage, restage or revert those blocks. You may still edit any file
   this block needs, including one an earlier block changed.
8. DECISION MATRIX — for each ambiguity or finding, route it yourself IN ORDER (first match wins):
  1. Not a real problem / false positive → DROP + LOG.
  2. A pre-existing finding, at any tier, that the ZONE ROUTING above does not fix → DROP + LOG.
      Never fix it (regression risk).
  3. Stops the build/tests/verification → FIX it where the ZONE ROUTING above places the fix, or
      ESCALATE it (7) where that routing says to.
  4. A finding the ZONE ROUTING above fixes, at any tier, that does not conflict with the plan → FIX.
      A conflict with the plan still goes to 6a or 6b.
  5. Needed to satisfy the spec / wire this block in → FIX (an unreachable or incomplete block is not done).
      A piece the plan's prescribed text leaves out is this case, not a conflict, so it takes no amendment.
      An exception to a rule the plan states is a conflict (6a or 6b), never a left-out piece.
  6a. Conflicts with the plan AND you VERIFIED that what the plan PRESCRIBES is itself defective (you

      PRECEDENCE — that verified defect also outranks the "NO scope creep beyond the plan and the fixes the ZONE ROUTING below allows"
      instruction above and the CONVENTIONS rubric. Everywhere else the plan and the conventions

  6b. Conflicts with the plan, and you did not verify that the plan's prescription is defective

  8. Any other open choice: weigh its benefit (what it improves, and how likely an input reaches it)
      against its cost (diff size, regression risk, scope). Benefit clearly ahead → FIX. Benefit not
      clearly ahead, or a different block's work → DROP + LOG.
  • Every finding a review names ends FIXED, LOGGED to the DISMISSED file, AMENDED (6a) or ESCALATED (7),
